title: Everything I do to get HUGE (Split, Reps, Lifts)
summary: NH lays out his current program: the 'Berserker' aesthetic goal, his instinct-driven 'gentleman split' (flexible upper/lower, six days a week, supersets), and his full exercise menu with rep ranges for every muscle, now split between his home gym and a newly joined commercial gym. He also covers lessons on machines and weighted calisthenics, and his very slow lean bulk (5 lb in a year).
claims: His ideal is the 'Berserker' physique: big arms, forearms and chest, a strong core and tree-trunk legs; shoulders can be smaller as long as the biceps aren't overpowered
Going into 2024 his priorities are rounder shoulders (via vertical presses and isolation), gnarlier forearms, and the core (obliques and serratus)
When you're obsessed with a muscle group, give in to it; your best gains come where the passion is
He trains 6 days a week, 1.5-2 hours per session excluding warm-up, with flexible rest days (1-2 per week depending on fatigue)
The gentleman split is an upper/lower template you don't have to obey strictly (calves on upper day or upper back on lower day are fine), built from supersets with synergistic days
Make days synergistic: if you train triceps, train chest and shoulders that day too, since presses hit them anyway
He builds each day by instinct from a fixed exercise menu and slots to fill; he doesn't recommend this to novices or intermediates, whose instinct will betray them
Flexibility is earned: beginners follow strict programs, advanced lifters earn freedom, like painters who master formal training before going freestyle
Instinct-based programming requires logging lifts or an excellent memory
He now trains about 50% at home and 50% at a commercial gym, doing legs at home and things like pull-ups and overhead presses at the gym
Rep-range logic: low reps (6-10, 8-12) for lifts where he can grind safely, higher reps for lifts that are awkward to load or hurt the elbow
Triceps menu: straight-bar pushdowns 8-12, cross-body cable extensions 10-15, skull crushers EZ bar 8-12 or dumbbell 10-15, JM press with safety squat bar 8-12 or Smith 10-15
The JM press, picked up from Basement Bodybuilding, Alex Leonidas and Bald Omni-Man, has helped his elbow pain
He picks from the menu by need and feel; e.g. triceps twice a week for 8 total sets does not mean every exercise every week
Biceps: never go below about 4-6 reps; his lowest is close-grip EZ curls at 4-8
Preacher variations with rope, towel, dumbbell, fat grip or EZ bar are 'soft' variations of one exercise, not too many exercises
He now does incline curls on cables and spider curls 10-15, because full range of motion may ease his elbow pain, despite favouring the 90-degree angle
Varying rep ranges matters for progression and freshness
He high-bar squats for 3 reps only about once a month to gauge strength; the squat is an accessory to his split squat, not the reverse
Quad split squat 8-12: front foot close, knee travels past the toes; a far foot turns it into a glute/hamstring exercise
Paused safety-bar squat 4-8 is his hardest squat, yet very safe

Belt squats and heels-elevated squats should be done with elevated heels and knees forward to reduce posterior chain and keep the stimulus on the quads; loading 300 lb with short reps defeats the purpose
He deadlifts 3 reps about once a month as an accessory to the RDL
Good mornings 6-10 never hurt his back and thicken the hamstrings and upper back; hyperextensions 8-12 are a safe, deep-stretch alternative
The RDL is his king of posterior-chain growth; so stimulating he only does it 2-3 times a month, for 6-12 reps
Usually 3-4 sets per exercise, sometimes only 2 when the stimulus is clearly reached
If a set falls below the rep range (e.g. 7 then 6 in a 6-10 range), he drops the next set and wins it back next session
Rotating connected variations (RDL, good morning, hyperextension) won't detrain the pattern; fear of regressing drives the spam-squats-and-deadlifts mentality
A lower day: slot A knee flexion + knee extension, slot B hip hinge, then neck and calves; with legs 3x/week he can't afford to destroy himself each session

Forearms: riser curls (cable hammer), reverse curls 6-12, pronation twists into the body, and wrist roller for flexion/extension; don't do the roller with arms straight out because it taxes the shoulders
Abs: decline sit-ups 6-10, flat 8-12, machine crunches 10-15, suitcase deadlifts and twists for the obliques
Calves: standing raises 8-12, seated EZ-bar raises 10-15, heavy dumbbell block raises 15-20, three times a week; calf raises reign supreme
Shoulders: standing military press 6-10 from low on the chest with a pause, and seated Smith press with a wider grip, no pause, stopping below the chin
He does lateral raises only on cables, pin at hip level: no trap takeover, no AC joint stress, no cheating; he can train them every week
Rear delt rows with a rope 8-15 at home
Neck: harness neck curls lying on a preacher bench and neck extensions seated; the harness was far better than plates or bands
Traps need little direct work since RDLs hit them; his only trap lift, belt-squat shrugs 10-15, is a guilty pleasure
Lats: weighted pull-ups 3-5, ring rows 6-10, dumbbell pullovers 6-10, machine pullovers, belt-squat/dumbbell rows, cable pulldowns 8-12, machine 10-15, diagonal pull
After years of bodyweight pull-ups he used a 45 lb plate on weighted pull-ups within a month; bodyweight carries over hugely
Never compare yourself with the average gym-goer; the average person sucks
He dropped close-grip bench: it gave him elbow tendinitis and pain at the back of the shoulder (felt like humeral subluxation) despite being safe for the front delt/rotator cuff
Chest is now weighted dips, weighted decline ring push-ups with a plate-loaded backpack, and cable/dumbbell/machine flies
Most blind spots are self-created; he only now realised he should load ring push-ups, which he ranks first in his hypertrophy tier list
He uses a broad exercise selection but low variation: soft variations of the same pattern prevent overuse injuries without changing the pattern
In a commercial gym you can superset by pairing a station with something portable, e.g. a press on a machine and dumbbell curls
At the commercial gym he trains 7 upper muscles with 6 exercises, skipping the most tired muscle; usually one exercise per muscle per day because he trains so often
If you can grow on as little as possible, do it; you keep room to add volume later
At home he does giant sets of 3-4 exercises in a row
Machines are great for isolating muscle and sparing tendons with little weight; most people misuse them with too much weight and no range of motion
Cable triceps work is better for joint health; his elbow tendinitis is almost gone
Once you reach about 15-20 clean pull-ups or 30 clean dips, stop bodyweight work and add load; 10 clean pull-ups typically means 10-20 lb for sets of 3-5
He has bulked for a year and gained 5 lb (from 210), under 0.5 lb a month; advanced lifters gaining 2 lb a month are just gaining fat
He'd rather gain 5 lb a year for five years and let the body set his limit; slight surplus, never hungry, hitting PRs
Training makes the biggest difference to a physique, far more than the diet
